description:
pkix-lint/src/deviation.rs:978-1001 (find_deviation) and 1021-1041 (find_deviation_for_chain) implement 'pick the matching deviation with highest priority, ties broken by insertion order' as a manual `for d in &self.deviations` loop with an `Option<&Deviation>` accumulator. This is what `Iterator::max_by_key` does, with the only twist being the tie-break rule.

The rustdoc explicitly notes 'max_by_key on (priority, -index) would also work', then chooses the manual fold anyway because `Iterator::max_by_key` returns the LAST element with the max key on ties, not the first. That subtle docs-API contract is the actual reason to write the manual loop — but the loop body would be more compact and obviously-correct as:

```rust
self.deviations
    .iter()
    .filter(|d| d.target_lint == lint_id && d.applies_to(cert, now_unix))
    .min_by_key(|d| (Reverse(d.priority), ...stable insertion-order tiebreaker via enumerate...))
```

Or more directly: `max_by_key` with negated priority and zip-with-index. The manual loop is correct but the explanatory comment 'max_by_key on (priority, -index) would also work, but iter().enumerate() lets us tie-break by insertion order' is misleading — the iter()+enumerate solution would also work, the author just chose the manual fold.

Idiom claim: when the answer is 'pick max element by key with a non-default tie-break', the idiomatic shape is `Iterator::min_by_key(|x| (Reverse(key(x)), index(x)))`. The manual loop signals to the reader that something unusual is happening when nothing is.

Duplicated across two methods (find_deviation, find_deviation_for_chain) — extract a helper or convert both to iterator chains. Filed as P3 chore; not a correctness issue.
title: DeviationStore::find_deviation and find_deviation_for_chain reimplement max_by_key with manual fold
